properties.description:
HLSTAE

This product covers eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia.

**HURRICANE HUNTERS FIND THAT ISAIAS NOW HAS 100 MPH WINDS**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- The Tropical Storm Warning and Hurricane Watch have been
upgraded to a Hurricane Warning for Central Walton and North
Walton

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Hurricane Warning is in effect for Central Walton and North
Walton
- A Storm Surge Warning and Hurricane Warning are in effect for
Coastal Bay and South Walton
- A Storm Surge Warning and Tropical Storm Warning are in effect
for Coastal Franklin, Coastal Gulf, Coastal Jefferson, and
Coastal Wakulla
- A Storm Surge Warning is in effect for Coastal Dixie and
Coastal Taylor
- A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for Calhoun, Clay,
Coffee, Dale, Decatur, Early, Gadsden, Geneva, Henry, Holmes,
Houston, Inland Bay, Inland Franklin, Inland Gulf, Inland
Wakulla, Jackson, Leon, Miller, Northern Liberty, Seminole,
Southern Liberty, and Washington
- A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for Baker, Calhoun,
Colquitt, Dougherty, Grady, Inland Jefferson, Lee, Mitchell,
Quitman, Randolph, Terrell, Thomas, and Worth

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 450 miles south-southwest of Panama City or about 450
miles southwest of Apalachicola
- 24.4N 89.3W
- Storm Intensity 100 mph
- Movement Northeast or 50 degrees at 12 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

...INLAND WALTON COUNTY UPGRADED TO HURRICANE WARNING...
...CONSIDERABLE FLOODING RAIN THREAT EXPECTED FOR FLORIDA PANHANDLE...

At 5 PM ET, Hurricane Isaias was located in the southern Gulf with
maximum sustained winds of 100 mph and moving NE at 12 mph. There are
overall no significant changes in the forecast reasoning from the
previous advisory. Isaias is forecast to turn northward in the next
day or so and accelerate in forward speed towards the central Gulf
coast. Additional strengthening is anticipated through tonight, and
may be near major hurricane strength prior to landfall. The wind field
is expected to expand considerably and may be lopsided towards the
east, which means impacts are likely well beyond the forecast cone,
particularly east of the hurricane's center.

Conditions could begin to deteriorate across the Florida Panhandle as
early as Friday morning. Therefore, residents are urged to finalize
their preparations today and early tomorrow.

Given the expected large size of Isaias as it nears northern Gulf
coast, the wind threat may extend well into the eastern portions of
the Tri-state area. An expected fast forward speed may also lead to
the wind threat extending further inland, especially near the core of
the storm. A Storm Surge Warning remains in effect from the all of our
Panhandle and Big Bend coast. Life-threatening inundation values of
5 to 7 feet above normally dry ground are forecast across the coastal
Panhandle to Indian Pass, 4 to 6 feet from Indian Pass to the
Steinhatchee River, and 3 to 5 feet from the Steinhatchee River to
Suwannee River, coincident with the high tide. The greatest surge risk
will be Friday into Saturday.

Soggy conditions across the region from recent rainfall will make much
of the Tri-state area more sensitive to flooding from additional heavy
rainfall from Isaias. Forecast rainfall totals of 4 to 8 inches is
expected across much of the area. Localized totals up to 15 inches are
possible, especially within banding across the Florida Panhandle and
Big Bend. If realized, these values are likely to produce isolated to
scattered flash flooding and some river flooding. Localized
considerable flash flooding is also possible where bands of heavy rain
move repeatedly over the same area. Given these factors, a Flood Watch
was issued for counties along and west of the I-75 corridor, the FL
Big Bend, and eastern FL Big Bend from Friday afternoon through
Saturday evening. Isaias will also bring an moderate chance for
several tornadoes across the Florida Panhandle and western FL Big Bend
on Friday into Saturday and Southeast AL & Southwest GA late Friday
into Saturday.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* FLOODING RAIN:
Protect against life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
extensive impacts across the area, especially over the Florida
Panhandle and Big Bend. Potential impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, and ditches may become
dangerous rivers. Flood control systems and barriers may become
stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.
Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

Protect against dangerous rainfall flooding having possible
significant impacts across elsewhere across the area.

* SURGE:
Protect against life-threatening surge having possible extensive
impacts across the coastal Florida Panhandle and Big Bend. Potential
impacts in this area include:
- Large areas of deep inundation with storm surge flooding
accentuated by battering waves. Structural damage to buildings,
with several washing away. Damage compounded by floating
debris. Locations may be uninhabitable for an extended period.
- Large sections of near-shore escape routes and secondary roads
washed out or severely flooded. Flood control systems and
barriers may become stressed.
- Severe beach erosion with significant dune loss.
- Major damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks, and piers. Many
small craft broken away from moorings, especially in
unprotected anchorages with some lifted onshore and stranded.

Elsewhere across eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia, little to no impact is
anticipated.

* TORNADOES:
Protect against a dangerous tornado event having possible significant
impacts across the area. Potential impacts include:
- The occurrence of scattered tornadoes can hinder the execution
of emergency plans during tropical events.
- Several places may experience tornado damage with a few spots
of considerable damage, power loss, and communications failures.
- Locations could realize roofs torn off frame houses, mobile
homes demolished, boxcars overturned, large trees snapped or
uprooted, vehicles tumbled, and small boats tossed about.
Dangerous projectiles can add to the toll.

Protect against a tornado event having possible limited impacts
for areas east of the I-75 corridor and the SE Florida Big Bend.

* WIND:
Protect against dangerous wind having possible significant impacts
across the Florida Panhandle. Potential impacts in this area include:
- Some damage to roofing and siding materials, along with damage
to porches, awnings, carports, and sheds. A few buildings
experiencing window, door, and garage door failures. Mobile
homes damaged, especially if unanchored. Unsecured lightweight
objects become dangerous projectiles.
- Several large trees snapped or uprooted, but with greater
numbers in places where trees are shallow rooted. Several
fences and roadway signs blown over.
- Some roads impassable from large debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places. A few bridges, causeways, and access
routes impassable.
- Scattered power and communications outages, but more prevalent
in areas with above ground lines.

Also, protect against hazardous wind having possible limited impacts
across the western Big Bend, and portions of Southwest Georgia.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to complete all preparations to protect life and
property in accordance with your emergency plan. Ensure you are in a
safe location before the onset of strong winds or possible flooding.

If you are relocating to safe shelter, leave as early as possible.
Allow extra time to reach your destination. Many roads and bridges
will be closed once strong winds arrive. Check the latest weather
forecast before departing and drive with caution.

If heading to a community shelter, become familiar with the shelter
rules before arrival, especially if you have special needs or have
pets. Take essential items with you from your Emergency Supplies Kit.

Failure to adequately shelter may result in serious injury or loss of
life. Always heed the advice of local officials and comply with any
orders that are issued. Remember, during the storm 9 1 1 Emergency
Services may not be able to immediately respond if conditions are
unsafe. This should be a big factor in your decision making.

Keep cell phones well charged. Cell phone chargers for automobiles
can be helpful, but be aware of your risk for deadly carbon monoxide
poisoning if your car is left idling in a garage or other poorly
ventilated area.

If you are a visitor, be sure to know the name of the city in which
you are staying and the name of the county in which it resides.
Listen for these locations in local news updates. Pay attention for
instructions from local authorities.

Storm surge is the leading killer associated with tropical storms and
hurricanes! Make sure you are in a safe area away from the surge
zone. Even if you are not in a surge-prone area, you could find
yourself cutoff by flood waters during and after the storm. Heed
evacuation orders issued by the local authorities.

Rapidly rising flood waters are deadly. If you are in a flood-prone
area, consider moving to higher ground. Never drive through a flooded
roadway. Remember, turn around don't drown!

If a Tornado Warning is issued for your area, be ready to shelter
quickly, preferably away from windows and in an interior room not
prone to flooding. If driving, scan the roadside for quick shelter
options.

If in a place that is vulnerable to high wind, such as near large
trees, a manufactured home, upper floors of a high-rise building, or
on a boat, consider moving to a safer shelter before the onset of
strong winds or flooding.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather radio or local news outlets
for official storm information. Be ready to adapt to possible changes
to the forecast. Ensure you have multiple ways to receive weather
warnings.


* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Tallahassee FL around 11 PM EDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

HLSTAE

This product covers eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia.

**ISAIAS STRONGER**
**PREPARATIONS TO PROTECT LIFE AND PROPERTY FROM STORM SURGE AND
DAMAGING WINDS IN THE WARNING AREA SHOULD BE RUSHED TO COMPLETION
TODAY**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- The Storm Surge Watch has been upgraded to a Storm Surge
Warning for Coastal Dixie
- A Tropical Storm Warning has been issued for Clay, Decatur,
Early, Gadsden, Leon, Miller, and Seminole
- A Tropical Storm Watch has been issued for Baker, Calhoun,
Colquitt, Dougherty, Grady, Inland Jefferson, Lee, Mitchell,
Quitman, Randolph, Terrell, Thomas, and Worth

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Storm Surge Warning and Hurricane Warning are in effect for
Coastal Bay and South Walton
- A Tropical Storm Warning and Hurricane Watch are in effect for
Central Walton and North Walton
- A Storm Surge Warning and Tropical Storm Warning are in effect
for Coastal Franklin, Coastal Gulf, Coastal Jefferson, and
Coastal Wakulla
- A Storm Surge Warning is in effect for Coastal Dixie and
Coastal Taylor
- A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for Calhoun, Clay,
Coffee, Dale, Decatur, Early, Gadsden, Geneva, Henry, Holmes,
Houston, Inland Bay, Inland Franklin, Inland Gulf, Inland
Wakulla, Jackson, Leon, Miller, Northern Liberty, Seminole,
Southern Liberty, and Washington
- A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for Baker, Calhoun,
Colquitt, Dougherty, Grady, Inland Jefferson, Lee, Mitchell,
Quitman, Randolph, Terrell, Thomas, and Worth

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 520 miles south-southwest of Panama City or about 520
miles southwest of Apalachicola
- 23.7N 90.2W
- Storm Intensity 85 mph
- Movement East-northeast or 60 degrees at 10 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

...NEW TROPICAL STORM WARNINGS IN EFFECT FOR FLORIDA BIG BEND AND PORTIONS OF
SOUTHWEST GEORGIA...
...NEW TROPICAL STORM WATCHES FOR JEFFERSON COUNTY
AND SOUTH-CENTRAL GEORGIA COUNTIES...
...STORM SURGE WARNING FOR DIXIE
COUNTY...

At 11 AM ET, Hurricane Isaias was located in the southern Gulf with
maximum sustained winds of 85 mph and moving ENE at 10 mph. There are
overall no significant changes in the forecast reasoning from the
previous advisory. Isaias is forecast to turn northward in the next
day or so and accelerate in forward speed towards the central Gulf
coast. Additional strengthening is anticipated through tonight, and
may be near major hurricane strength prior to landfall. The wind field
is expected to expand considerably and may be lopsided towards the
east, which means impacts are likely well beyond the forecast cone,
particularly east of the hurricane's center. Tropical Storm Warnings
have been expanded east to include Florida counties: Leon and Gadsden.
Tropical Storm Warnings for Georgia counties: Decatur, Seminole,
Miller, Early, and Clay. The Tropical Storm Watch includes our Georgia
counties: Quitman, Randolph, Terrell, Lee, Calhoun, Dougherty, Worth,
Baker, Mitchell, Colquitt, Grady, and Thomas. There is a Tropical
Storm Watch for Jefferson County in Florida.

Conditions could begin to deteriorate across the Florida Panhandle as
early as Friday morning. Therefore, residents are urged to finalize
their preparations today and early tomorrow.

Given the expected large size of Isaias as it nears northern Gulf
coast, the wind threat may extend well into the eastern portions of
the Tri-state area. An expected fast forward speed may also lead to
the wind threat extending further inland, especially near the core of
the storm. A Storm Surge Warning remains in effect from the all of our
Panhandle and Big Bend coast. Life-threatening inundation values of
5 to 7 feet above normally dry ground are forecast across the coastal
Panhandle to Indian Pass, 4 to 6 feet from Indian Pass to the
Steinhatchee River, and 3 to 5 feet from the Steinhatchee River to
Suwannee River, coincident with the high tide. The greatest surge risk
will be Friday into Saturday.

Soggy conditions across the region from recent rainfall will make much
of the Tri-state area more sensitive to flooding from additional heavy
rainfall from Isaias. Forecast rainfall totals of 3 to 7 inches is
expected across much of the area, with higher amounts of 10 inches
with isolated amounts up to 15 inches. If realized, these values are
likely to produce isolated to scattered flash flooding and some river
flooding. Localized considerable flash flooding is also possible where
bands of heavy rain move repeatedly over the same area. Given these
factors, a Flood Watch was issued for counties west of the
I-75 corridor and Eastern FL Big Bend from Friday afternoon until
Saturday evening. Isaias will also bring an elevated chance for
several tornadoes across the Florida Panhandle and Western FL Big Bend
on Friday into Saturday and Southeast AL & Southwest GA late Friday
into Saturday.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* FLOODING RAIN:
Protect against life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
extensive impacts across the Florida Panhandle, western Big Bend, SE
Alabama, and southwest Georgia.
Potential impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, and ditches may become
dangerous rivers. Flood control systems and barriers may become
stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.
Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

Protect against dangerous rainfall flooding having possible limited
to significant impacts elsewhere across the area.

* SURGE:
Protect against life-threatening surge having possible extensive
impacts across the coastal Florida Panhandle and Big Bend. Potential
impacts in this area include:
- Large areas of deep inundation with storm surge flooding
accentuated by battering waves. Structural damage to buildings,
with several washing away. Damage compounded by floating
debris. Locations may be uninhabitable for an extended period.
- Large sections of near-shore escape routes and secondary roads
washed out or severely flooded. Flood control systems and
barriers may become stressed.
- Severe beach erosion with significant dune loss.
- Major damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks, and piers. Many
small craft broken away from moorings, especially in
unprotected anchorages with some lifted onshore and stranded.

Elsewhere across eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia, little to no impact is
anticipated.

* TORNADOES:
Protect against a dangerous tornado event having possible significant
impacts across the area. Potential impacts include:
- The occurrence of scattered tornadoes can hinder the execution
of emergency plans during tropical events.
- Several places may experience tornado damage with a few spots
of considerable damage, power loss, and communications failures.
- Locations could realize roofs torn off frame houses, mobile
homes demolished, boxcars overturned, large trees snapped or
uprooted, vehicles tumbled, and small boats tossed about.
Dangerous projectiles can add to the toll.

Protect against a tornado event having possible limited impacts
across the extreme southeast Florida Big Bend.

* WIND:
Protect against dangerous wind having possible significant impacts
across the Florida Panhandle.
Potential impacts in this area include:
- Some damage to roofing and siding materials, along with damage
to porches, awnings, carports, and sheds. A few buildings
experiencing window, door, and garage door failures. Mobile
homes damaged, especially if unanchored. Unsecured lightweight
objects become dangerous projectiles.
- Several large trees snapped or uprooted, but with greater
numbers in places where trees are shallow rooted. Several
fences and roadway signs blown over.
- Some roads impassable from large debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places. A few bridges, causeways, and access
routes impassable.
- Scattered power and communications outages, but more prevalent
in areas with above ground lines.

Also, protect against hazardous wind having possible limited impacts
across the western Big Bend, and portions of Southwest Georgia.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials


* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to complete all preparations to protect life and
property in accordance with your emergency plan. Ensure you are in a
safe location before the onset of strong winds or possible flooding.

If you are relocating to safe shelter, leave as early as possible.
Allow extra time to reach your destination. Many roads and bridges
will be closed once strong winds arrive. Check the latest weather
forecast before departing and drive with caution.

If heading to a community shelter, become familiar with the shelter
rules before arrival, especially if you have special needs or have
pets. Take essential items with you from your Emergency Supplies Kit.

Failure to adequately shelter may result in serious injury or loss of
life. Always heed the advice of local officials and comply with any
orders that are issued. Remember, during the storm 9 1 1 Emergency
Services may not be able to immediately respond if conditions are
unsafe. This should be a big factor in your decision making.

Keep cell phones well charged. Cell phone chargers for automobiles
can be helpful, but be aware of your risk for deadly carbon monoxide
poisoning if your car is left idling in a garage or other poorly
ventilated area.

If you are a visitor, be sure to know the name of the city in which
you are staying and the name of the county in which it resides.
Listen for these locations in local news updates. Pay attention for
instructions from local authorities.

Storm surge is the leading killer associated with tropical storms and
hurricanes! Make sure you are in a safe area away from the surge
zone. Even if you are not in a surge-prone area, you could find
yourself cutoff by flood waters during and after the storm. Heed
evacuation orders issued by the local authorities.

Rapidly rising flood waters are deadly. If you are in a flood-prone
area, consider moving to higher ground. Never drive through a flooded
roadway. Remember, turn around don't drown!

If a Tornado Warning is issued for your area, be ready to shelter
quickly, preferably away from windows and in an interior room not
prone to flooding. If driving, scan the roadside for quick shelter
options.

If in a place that is vulnerable to high wind, such as near large
trees, a manufactured home, upper floors of a high-rise building, or
on a boat, consider moving to a safer shelter before the onset of
strong winds or flooding.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather radio or local news outlets
for official storm information. Be ready to adapt to possible changes
to the forecast. Ensure you have multiple ways to receive weather
warnings.


* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Tallahassee FL around 5 PM EDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

rainfall from Isaias. Forecast rainfall totals of 3 to 7 inches is
expected across much of the area, with isolated amounts in excess of 10
inches. If realized, these values are likely to produce isolated to
scattered flash flooding and some river flooding. Localized
considerable flash flooding is also possible where bands of heavy rain
move repeatedly over the same area. Given these factors, a Flood Watch
was issued for counties west of the I- 75 corridor and Eastern FL Big
Bend from Friday afternoon until Saturday evening. Isaias will also
bring an elevated chance for several tornadoes across the Florida
Panhandle and Western FL Big Bend on Friday into Saturday and Southeast
AL & Southwest GA late Friday into Saturday.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* FLOODING RAIN:
Protect against life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
extensive impacts across the Florida Panhandle, western Big Bend, and
SE Alabama. Potential impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, and ditches may become
dangerous rivers. Flood control systems and barriers may become
stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.
Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

Protect against dangerous rainfall flooding having possible limited
to significant impacts elsewhere across the area.

* SURGE:
Protect against life-threatening surge having possible extensive
impacts across the coastal Florida Panhandle and Big Bend. Potential
impacts in this area include:
- Large areas of deep inundation with storm surge flooding
accentuated by battering waves. Structural damage to buildings,
with several washing away. Damage compounded by floating
debris. Locations may be uninhabitable for an extended period.
- Large sections of near-shore escape routes and secondary roads
washed out or severely flooded. Flood control systems and
barriers may become stressed.
- Severe beach erosion with significant dune loss.
- Major damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks, and piers. Many
small craft broken away from moorings, especially in
unprotected anchorages with some lifted onshore and stranded.

Elsewhere across eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia, little to no impact is
anticipated.

* WIND:
Protect against dangerous wind having possible significant impacts
across the Florida Panhandle. Potential impacts in this area
include:
- Some damage to roofing and siding materials, along with damage
to porches, awnings, carports, and sheds. A few buildings
experiencing window, door, and garage door failures. Mobile
homes damaged, especially if unanchored. Unsecured lightweight
objects become dangerous projectiles.
- Several large trees snapped or uprooted, but with greater
numbers in places where trees are shallow rooted. Several
fences and roadway signs blown over.
- Some roads impassable from large debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places. A few bridges, causeways, and access
routes impassable.
- Scattered power and communications outages, but more prevalent
in areas with above ground lines.

Also, protect against hazardous wind having possible limited impacts
across the Florida Big Bend and southeast Alabama.

Elsewhere across eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia, little to no impact is
anticipated.

* TORNADOES:
Protect against a dangerous tornado event having possible significant
impacts across the area. Potential impacts
include:
- The occurrence of scattered tornadoes can hinder the execution
of emergency plans during tropical events.
- Several places may experience tornado damage with a few spots
of considerable damage, power loss, and communications failures.
- Locations could realize roofs torn off frame houses, mobile
homes demolished, boxcars overturned, large trees snapped or
uprooted, vehicles tumbled, and small boats tossed about.
Dangerous projectiles can add to the toll.


PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials


* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to complete all preparations to protect life and
property in accordance with your emergency plan. Ensure you are in a
safe location before the onset of strong winds or possible flooding.

If you are relocating to safe shelter, leave as early as possible.
Allow extra time to reach your destination. Many roads and bridges
will be closed once strong winds arrive. Check the latest weather
forecast before departing and drive with caution.

If heading to a community shelter, become familiar with the shelter
rules before arrival, especially if you have special needs or have
pets. Take essential items with you from your Emergency Supplies Kit.

Keep cell phones well charged. Cell phone chargers for automobiles
can be helpful, but be aware of your risk for deadly carbon monoxide
poisoning if your car is left idling in a garage or other poorly
ventilated area.

If you are a visitor, be sure to know the name of the city in which
you are staying and the name of the county in which it resides.
Listen for these locations in local news updates. Pay attention for
instructions from local authorities.

Storm surge is the leading killer associated with tropical storms and
hurricanes! Make sure you are in a safe area away from the surge
zone. Even if you are not in a surge-prone area, you could find
yourself cutoff by flood waters during and after the storm. Heed
evacuation orders issued by the local authorities.

Rapidly rising flood waters are deadly. If you are in a flood-prone
area, consider moving to higher ground. Never drive through a flooded
roadway. Remember, turn around don't drown!

If a Tornado Warning is issued for your area, be ready to shelter
quickly, preferably away from windows and in an interior room not
prone to flooding. If driving, scan the roadside for quick shelter
options.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather radio or local news outlets
for official storm information. Be ready to adapt to possible changes
to the forecast. Ensure you have multiple ways to receive weather
warnings.


* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Tallahassee FL around 11 AM ET, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

expected to expand considerably and may be lopsided towards the east,
which means impacts are likely well beyond the forecast cone,
particularly east of the hurricane's center. Inland FL counties have
now been upgraded from a Tropical Storm Watch to Warning, including
Liberty, Franklin, and Wakulla Counties. Conditions could begin to
deteriorate across the Florida Panhandle as early as Friday morning.

early tomorrow.

properties.description:
HLSTAE

This product covers eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend, southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia

**HURRICANE, STORM SURGE, TROPICAL STORM WARNINGS NOW IN EFFECT FOR
MOST COASTAL LOCATIONS**

NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- The Hurricane Watch has been upgraded to a Hurricane Warning
and the Storm Surge Watch has been upgraded to a Storm Surge
Warning for Coastal Bay and South Walton
- The Storm Surge Watch has been upgraded to a Storm Surge
Warning and the Hurricane Watch has been upgraded to a Tropical
Storm Warning for Coastal Gulf
- The Storm Surge Watch has been upgraded to a Storm Surge
Warning and the Tropical Storm Watch has been upgraded to a
Tropical Storm Warning for Coastal Franklin, Coastal Jefferson,
and Coastal Wakulla
- The Storm Surge Watch has been upgraded to a Storm Surge
Warning for Coastal Taylor
- A Tropical Storm Watch has been issued for Inland Wakulla

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Storm Surge Warning and Hurricane Warning are in effect for
Coastal Bay and South Walton
- A Storm Surge Warning and Tropical Storm Warning are in effect
for Coastal Franklin, Coastal Gulf, Coastal Jefferson, and
Coastal Wakulla
- A Storm Surge Warning is in effect for Coastal Taylor
- A Hurricane Watch is in effect for Central Walton and North
Walton
- A Storm Surge Watch is in effect for Coastal Dixie
- A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for Calhoun, Coffee, Dale,
Geneva, Henry, Holmes, Houston, Inland Bay, Inland Franklin,
Inland Gulf, Inland Wakulla, Jackson, Northern Liberty,
Southern Liberty, and Washington

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 630 miles southwest of Panama City or about 640 miles
southwest of Apalachicola
- 22.9N 91.9W
- Storm Intensity 70 mph
- Movement East-northeast or 70 degrees at 9 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

At 11 PM ET, Tropical Storm Isaias was located in the southern Gulf
with maximum sustained winds of 70 mph and moving ENE at 9 mph. Isaias
is forecast to turn northward in the next day or so and accelerate in
forward speed towards the central Gulf coast. Steady strengthening is
expected the day or so, although some weakening is forecast just prior
to landfall. The wind field is expected to expand considerably and may
be lopsided towards the east, leading to windier conditions for the
western portions of our area. There is still uncertainty with both
timing and track. Conditions could begin to deteriorate across the
Florida Panhandle as early as Friday morning.

Given the expected large size of Isaias as it nears land, the wind
threat may extend well into the eastern portions of our area. An
expected fast forward speed may also lead to the wind threat extending
further inland, especially near the core of the storm. A Storm Surge
Warning is now in effect from the Steinhatchee River west to the
Okaloosa/Walton County line. Inundation values of 5 to 7 feet above
normally dry ground are forecast across the coastal Panhandle to
Indian Pass, 4 to 6 feet from Indian Pass to the Steinhatchee River,
and 2 to 4 feet from the Steinhatchee River to Yankeetown.

Soggy conditions across the region from recent rainfall will make the
area more sensitive to flooding from additional heavy rainfall from
Isaias. Forecast rainfall totals of 3 to 7 inches is expected across
much of the area, with isolated amounts near 10 inches possible. If
realized, these values would likely cause at least isolated flash
flooding and some river flooding. Tropical Storm Isaias will also
bring an elevated chance for tornadoes across the Florida Panhandle on
Friday into Saturday and southeastern Alabama late Friday into
Saturday.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* FLOODING RAIN:
Protect against life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
extensive impacts across the Florida Panhandle and western Florida Big Bend.
Potential impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, and ditches may become
dangerous rivers. Flood control systems and barriers may become
stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.
Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

Protect against dangerous rainfall flooding having possible limited
to significant impacts across southeast Alabama, southwest Georgia, and
the eastern Florida Big Bend.

* WIND:
Protect against dangerous wind having possible significant impacts
across southeastern Alabama and the Florida Panhandle. Potential impacts
in this area include:
- Some damage to roofing and siding materials, along with damage
to porches, awnings, carports, and sheds. A few buildings
experiencing window, door, and garage door failures. Mobile
homes damaged, especially if unanchored. Unsecured lightweight
objects become dangerous projectiles.
- Several large trees snapped or uprooted, but with greater
numbers in places where trees are shallow rooted. Several
fences and roadway signs blown over.
- Some roads impassable from large debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places. A few bridges, causeways, and access
routes impassable.
- Scattered power and communications outages, but more prevalent
in areas with above ground lines.

Also, protect against hazardous wind having possible limited impacts
across the western Florida Big Bend and portions of far southwestern Georgia.

Elsewhere across southeastern Florida Big Bend, and much of southwestern Georgia,
little to no impact is anticipated.

* SURGE:
Protect against life-threatening surge having possible extensive
impacts across coastal Florida Panhandle and Florida Big Bend. Potential impacts in
this area include:
- Large areas of deep inundation with storm surge flooding
accentuated by battering waves. Structural damage to buildings,
with several washing away. Damage compounded by floating
debris. Locations may be uninhabitable for an extended period.
- Large sections of near-shore escape routes and secondary roads
washed out or severely flooded. Flood control systems and
barriers may become stressed.
- Severe beach erosion with significant dune loss.
- Major damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks, and piers. Many
small craft broken away from moorings, especially in
unprotected anchorages with some lifted onshore and stranded.

Elsewhere across inland portions of Florida Panhandle, inland portions of Florida Big
Bend, southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia, little to no impact is
anticipated.

* TORNADOES:
Protect against a tornado event having possible limited impacts
across the Florida Panhandle and southeastern Alabama. Potential impacts include:
- The occurrence of isolated tornadoes can hinder the execution
of emergency plans during tropical events.
- A few places may experience tornado damage, along with power
and communications disruptions.
- Locations could realize roofs peeled off buildings, chimneys
toppled, mobile homes pushed off foundations or overturned,
large tree tops and branches snapped off, shallow-rooted trees
knocked over, moving vehicles blown off roads, and small boats
pulled from moorings.

Elsewhere across the Florida Big Bend and southwestern Georgia, little to no impact
is anticipated, but we'll continue to monitor the potential over the next 48 hours.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to check your emergency plan and emergency supplies
kit and take necessary actions to protect your family and secure your
home or business.

When making safety and preparedness decisions, do not focus on the
exact forecast track since hazards such as flooding rain, damaging
wind gusts, storm surge, and tornadoes extend well away from the
center of the storm.

If you live in a place particularly vulnerable to flooding, such as
near the Gulf of America or a large inland lake, in a low-lying or
poor drainage area, or near an already swollen river, plan to move to
safe shelter on higher ground.

Always heed the advice of local officials and comply with orders that
are issued. Do not needlessly jeopardize your life or the lives of
others.

When securing your property, outside preparations should be concluded
as soon as possible before conditions deteriorate. The onset of
strong gusty winds or flooding can cause certain preparedness
activities to become unsafe.

Be sure to let friends and family members know of your intentions for
weathering the storm and your whereabouts. Have someone located away
from the threatened area serve as your point of contact. Share vital
contact information with others. Keep cell phones handy and charged.

Check on those who may not be fully aware of the situation or who are
unable to make personal preparations.

If you are a visitor, know the name of the county in which you are
located and where it is relative to current watches and warnings. If
staying at a hotel, ask the management staff about their onsite
disaster plan. Listen for evacuation orders, especially pertaining to
area visitors.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather Radio and local news
outlets for official storm information. Listen for possible changes
to the forecast.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Tallahassee FL around 6 AM EDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

properties.description:
HLSTAE

This product covers eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia

**ISAIAS QUICKLY INTENSIFYING, FORECAST TO BE A HURRICANE BY THURSDAY
MORNING**


NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Watch has been issued for Calhoun, Coffee,
Dale, Geneva, Henry, Houston, Inland Franklin, Jackson,
Northern Liberty, and Southern Liberty

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Storm Surge Watch and Hurricane Watch are in effect for
Coastal Bay, Coastal Gulf, and South Walton
- A Storm Surge Watch and Tropical Storm Watch are in effect for
Coastal Franklin, Coastal Jefferson, and Coastal Wakulla
- A Hurricane Watch is in effect for Central Walton and North
Walton
- A Storm Surge Watch is in effect for Coastal Dixie and Coastal
Taylor
- A Tropical Storm Watch is in effect for Calhoun, Coffee, Dale,
Geneva, Henry, Holmes, Houston, Inland Bay, Inland Franklin,
Inland Gulf, Jackson, Northern Liberty, Southern Liberty, and
Washington

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 680 miles southwest of Panama City or about 690 miles
southwest of Apalachicola
- 22.7N 92.9W
- Storm Intensity 65 mph
- Movement East-northeast or 65 degrees at 8 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

...TROPICAL STORM WATCH ISSUED FOR SOUTHEAST ALABAMA AND INLAND FLORIDA PANHANDLE
COUNTIES...

At 5 PM ET, Tropical Storm Isaias was still located in the Bay of
Campeche with maximum sustained winds of 65 mph and moving ENE at
8 mph. Isaias is forecast to turn northward in the next day or so and
accelerate in forward speed towards the central Gulf coast. Steady
strengthening is expected through much of the next couple of days,
although some weakening may be possible just before landfall. The wind
field is expected to expand considerably and may be lopsided towards
the east, leading to windier conditions for portions of our area.
There is still considerable uncertainty with both timing and track.
Conditions could begin to deteriorate across the Panhandle as early as
Friday morning.

Given the expected large size of Isaias, the wind threat may extend
well into the eastern portions of our area. An expected fast forward
speed may also lead to the wind threat extending further inland. Storm
surge will be possible along our whole coastline including the
Panhandle and Apalachee Bay. Inundation values of 5 to 7 feet above
ground level (AGL) are possible across the coastal Panhandle to Indian
Pass, 4 to 6 feet AGL from Indian Pass to the Steinhatchee River, and
2 to 4 feet AGL from the Steinhatchee River to Yankeetown.

Soggy conditions across the region from recent rainfall will make the
area more sensitive to flooding from additional heavy rainfall from
Isaias. Forecast rainfall totals of 3 to 7 inches is expected across
much of the area, with isolated amounts near 10 inches possible. If
realized, these values would likely cause at least isolated flash
flooding and some river flooding. It is too soon to determine exact
tornado impacts, but there is an elevated chance for tornadoes Friday
into Saturday.



POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* FLOODING RAIN:
Prepare for life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
extensive impacts across the Florida Panhandle and portions of SE
Alabama. Potential impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, and ditches may become
dangerous rivers. Flood control systems and barriers may become
stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.
Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

Prepare for dangerous rainfall flooding having possible limited to
significant impacts across southeast Alabama, southwest Georgia, and
the Florida Big Bend.

* WIND:
Prepare for dangerous wind having possible significant impacts across
Southeast Alabama and the Florida Panhandle. Potential impacts in this
area include:
- Some damage to roofing and siding materials, along with damage
to porches, awnings, carports, and sheds. A few buildings
experiencing window, door, and garage door failures. Mobile
homes damaged, especially if unanchored. Unsecured lightweight
objects become dangerous projectiles.
- Several large trees snapped or uprooted, but with greater
numbers in places where trees are shallow rooted. Several
fences and roadway signs blown over.
- Some roads impassable from large debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places. A few bridges, causeways, and access
routes impassable.
- Scattered power and communications outages, but more prevalent
in areas with above ground lines.

Also, prepare for hazardous wind having possible limited impacts
across the Florida Big Bend and Southeast Alabama.

Elsewhere across eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend, and
southwestern Georgia, little to no impact is anticipated.

* SURGE:
Prepare for life-threatening surge having possible extensive impacts
across coastal Florida Panhandle and Florida Big Bend. Potential
impacts in this area include:
- Large areas of deep inundation with storm surge flooding
accentuated by battering waves. Structural damage to buildings,
with several washing away. Damage compounded by floating
debris. Locations may be uninhabitable for an extended period.
- Large sections of near-shore escape routes and secondary roads
washed out or severely flooded. Flood control systems and
barriers may become stressed.
- Severe beach erosion with significant dune loss.
- Major damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks, and piers. Many
small craft broken away from moorings, especially in
unprotected anchorages with some lifted onshore and stranded.

Elsewhere across eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia, little to no impact is
anticipated.

* TORNADOES:
Prepare for a tornado event having possible limited impacts across the
Florida Panhandle. Potential impacts include:
- The occurrence of isolated tornadoes can hinder the execution
of emergency plans during tropical events.
- A few places may experience tornado damage, along with power
and communications disruptions.
- Locations could realize roofs peeled off buildings, chimneys
toppled, mobile homes pushed off foundations or overturned,
large tree tops and branches snapped off, shallow-rooted trees
knocked over, moving vehicles blown off roads, and small boats
pulled from moorings.

Elsewhere across eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia, little to no impact is
anticipated.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to check your emergency plan and emergency supplies
kit and take necessary actions to protect your family and secure your
home or business.

When making safety and preparedness decisions, do not focus on the
exact forecast track since hazards such as flooding rain, damaging
wind gusts, storm surge, and tornadoes extend well away from the
center of the storm.


If you live in a place particularly vulnerable to flooding, such as
near the Gulf of America or a large inland lake, in a low-lying or
poor drainage area, or near an already swollen river, plan to move to
safe shelter on higher ground.

Always heed the advice of local officials and comply with orders that
are issued. Do not needlessly jeopardize your life or the lives of
others.

When securing your property, outside preparations should be concluded
as soon as possible before conditions deteriorate. The onset of
strong gusty winds or flooding can cause certain preparedness
activities to become unsafe.

Be sure to let friends and family members know of your intentions for
weathering the storm and your whereabouts. Have someone located away
from the threatened area serve as your point of contact. Share vital
contact information with others. Keep cell phones handy and charged.

Check on those who may not be fully aware of the situation or who are
unable to make personal preparations.

If you are a visitor, know the name of the county in which you are
located and where it is relative to current watches and warnings. If
staying at a hotel, ask the management staff about their onsite
disaster plan. Listen for evacuation orders, especially pertaining to
area visitors.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather Radio and local news
outlets for official storm information. Listen for possible changes
to the forecast.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Tallahassee FL around 11 PM EDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, and ditches may become
dangerous rivers. Flood control systems and barriers may become
stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.
Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

Prepare for dangerous rainfall flooding having possible limited to
significant impacts across southeast Alabama, southwest Georgia, and
the Florida Big Bend.

* SURGE:
Prepare for life-threatening surge having possible extensive impacts
across the coastal Florida Panhandle and Florida Big Bend. Potential
impacts in this area include:
- Large areas of deep inundation with storm surge flooding
accentuated by battering waves. Structural damage to buildings,
with several washing away. Damage compounded by floating
debris. Locations may be uninhabitable for an extended period.
- Large sections of near-shore escape routes and secondary roads
washed out or severely flooded. Flood control systems and
barriers may become stressed.
- Severe beach erosion with significant dune loss.
- Major damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks, and piers. Many
small craft broken away from moorings, especially in
unprotected anchorages with some lifted onshore and stranded.

Elsewhere across eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia, little to no impact is
anticipated.

* WIND:
Prepare for dangerous wind having possible significant impacts across
the Florida Panhandle. Potential impacts in this area include:
- Some damage to roofing and siding materials, along with damage
to porches, awnings, carports, and sheds. A few buildings
experiencing window, door, and garage door failures. Mobile
homes damaged, especially if unanchored. Unsecured lightweight
objects become dangerous projectiles.
- Several large trees snapped or uprooted, but with greater
numbers in places where trees are shallow rooted. Several
fences and roadway signs blown over.
- Some roads impassable from large debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places. A few bridges, causeways, and access
routes impassable.
- Scattered power and communications outages, but more prevalent
in areas with above ground lines.

Also, prepare for hazardous wind having possible limited impacts
across the Florida Big Bend and Southeast Alabama.

Elsewhere across eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia, little to no impact is
anticipated.

* TORNADOES:
Little to no impacts are anticipated at this time
across eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend, southeastern
Alabama and southwestern Georgia.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials


* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to check your emergency plan and emergency supplies
kit and take necessary actions to protect your family and secure your
home or business.

When making safety and preparedness decisions, do not focus on the
exact forecast track since hazards such as flooding rain, damaging
wind gusts, storm surge, and tornadoes extend well away from the
center of the storm.

If you live in a place particularly vulnerable to flooding, such as
near the Gulf of America or a large inland lake, in a low-lying or
poor drainage area, or near an already swollen river, plan to move to
safe shelter on higher ground.

Always heed the advice of local officials and comply with orders that
are issued. Do not needlessly jeopardize your life or the lives of
others.

When securing your property, outside preparations should be concluded
as soon as possible before conditions deteriorate. The onset of
strong gusty winds or flooding can cause certain preparedness
activities to become unsafe.

Be sure to let friends and family members know of your intentions for
weathering the storm and your whereabouts. Have someone located away
from the threatened area serve as your point of contact. Share vital
contact information with others. Keep cell phones handy and charged.

Check on those who may not be fully aware of the situation or who are
unable to make personal preparations.

If you are a visitor, know the name of the county in which you are
located and where it is relative to current watches and warnings. If
staying at a hotel, ask the management staff about their onsite
disaster plan. Listen for evacuation orders, especially pertaining to
area visitors.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather Radio and local news
outlets for official storm information. Listen for possible changes
to the forecast.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Tallahassee FL around 5 PM EDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued October 7 at 11:27AM EDT by NWS Tallahassee FL
properties.description:
HLSTAE

This product covers eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend, southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia

**HURRICANE AND STORM SURGE WATCHES ISSUED FOR PORTIONS OF THE
NORTHERN GULF COAST FOR STRENGTHENING ISAIAS**


NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Storm Surge Watch and Hurricane Watch have been issued for
Coastal Bay, Coastal Gulf, and South Walton
- A Storm Surge Watch and Tropical Storm Watch have been issued
for Coastal Franklin, Coastal Jefferson, and Coastal Wakulla
- A Storm Surge Watch has been issued for Coastal Dixie and
Coastal Taylor

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Storm Surge Watch and Hurricane Watch are in effect for
Coastal Bay, Coastal Gulf, and South Walton
- A Storm Surge Watch and Tropical Storm Watch are in effect for
Coastal Franklin, Coastal Jefferson, and Coastal Wakulla
- A Storm Surge Watch is in effect for Coastal Dixie and Coastal
Taylor

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 720 miles southwest of Panama City or about 730 miles
southwest of Apalachicola
- 22.4N 93.6W
- Storm Intensity 45 mph
- Movement East-northeast or 70 degrees at 8 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

...ISAIAS IS FORECAST TO STRENGTHEN AS IT APPROACHES THE CENTRAL GULF COAST
LATE THIS WEEK...

At 11 AM ET, Tropical Storm Isaias was still located in the Bay of
Campeche and moving ENE at 8 mph. Isaias is forecast to turn northward
in the next day or so and accelerate in forward speed towards the
central Gulf coast. Steady strengthening is expected through much of the
next couple of days, although some weakening may be possible just before
landfall. The wind field is expected to expand considerably and may be
lopsided towards the east, leading to windier conditions for portions of
our area. There is still considerable uncertainty with both timing and
track. Conditions could begin to deteriorate across the Panhandle as
early as Friday morning.

Given the expected large size of Isaias, the wind threat may extend well
into the eastern portions of our area. An expected fast forward speed
may also lead to the wind threat extending further inland. Storm surge
will be possible along our whole coastline including the Panhandle and
Apalachee Bay. Inundation values of 5 to 7 feet above ground level (AGL)
are possible across the coastal Panhandle to Indian Pass, 3 to 5 feet AGL
from Indian Pass to the Aucilla River, and 2 to 4 feet AGL from the
Aucilla River to Yankeetown.

Soggy conditions across the region from recent rainfall will make the area
more sensitive to flooding from additional heavy rainfall from Isaias.
Forecast rainfall totals of 3 to 6 inches is expected across much of the
area, with isolated amounts near 10 inches possible. If realized, these
values would likely cause at least isolated flash flooding and some river
flooding. It is too soon to determine exact tornado impacts, if any, but
a few cannot be ruled out at this time.


POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* FLOODING RAIN:
Prepare for life-threatening rainfall flooding having possible
extensive impacts across the FL Panhandle. Potential
impacts include:
- Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may rapidly overflow their banks in
multiple places. Small streams, creeks, and ditches may become
dangerous rivers. Flood control systems and barriers may become
stressed.
- Flood waters can enter many structures within multiple
communities, some structures becoming uninhabitable or washed
away. Many places where flood waters may cover escape routes.
Streets and parking lots become rivers of moving water with
underpasses submerged. Driving conditions become dangerous.
Many road and bridge closures with some weakened or washed out.

Prepare for dangerous rainfall flooding having possible limited to
significant impacts across southeast Alabama, southwest Georgia, and
the Florida Big Bend.

* SURGE:
Prepare for life-threatening surge having possible extensive impacts
across the coastal Florida Panhandle and Florida Big Bend. Potential
impacts in this area include:
- Large areas of deep inundation with storm surge flooding
accentuated by battering waves. Structural damage to buildings,
with several washing away. Damage compounded by floating
debris. Locations may be uninhabitable for an extended period.
- Large sections of near-shore escape routes and secondary roads
washed out or severely flooded. Flood control systems and
barriers may become stressed.
- Severe beach erosion with significant dune loss.
- Major damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks, and piers. Many
small craft broken away from moorings, especially in
unprotected anchorages with some lifted onshore and stranded.

Elsewhere across eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia, little to no impact is
anticipated.

* WIND:
Prepare for dangerous wind having possible significant impacts across
the Florida Panhandle. Potential impacts in this area include:
- Some damage to roofing and siding materials, along with damage
to porches, awnings, carports, and sheds. A few buildings
experiencing window, door, and garage door failures. Mobile
homes damaged, especially if unanchored. Unsecured lightweight
objects become dangerous projectiles.
- Several large trees snapped or uprooted, but with greater
numbers in places where trees are shallow rooted. Several
fences and roadway signs blown over.
- Some roads impassable from large debris, and more within urban
or heavily wooded places. A few bridges, causeways, and access
routes impassable.
- Scattered power and communications outages, but more prevalent
in areas with above ground lines.

Also, prepare for hazardous wind having possible limited impacts
across the Florida Big Bend and Southeast Alabama.

Elsewhere across eastern Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend,
southeastern Alabama and southwestern Georgia, little to no impact is
anticipated.

* TORNADOES:
Little to no impacts are anticipated at this time across eastern
Florida panhandle, Florida Big Bend, southeastern Alabama and
southwestern Georgia.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to check your emergency plan and emergency supplies
kit and take necessary actions to protect your family and secure your
home or business.

When making safety and preparedness decisions, do not focus on the
exact forecast track since hazards such as flooding rain, damaging
wind gusts, storm surge, and tornadoes extend well away from the
center of the storm.

If you live in a place particularly vulnerable to flooding, such as
near the Gulf of America or a large inland lake, in a low-lying or
poor drainage area, or near an already swollen river, plan to move to
safe shelter on higher ground.

Always heed the advice of local officials and comply with orders that
are issued. Do not needlessly jeopardize your life or the lives of
others.

When securing your property, outside preparations should be concluded
as soon as possible before conditions deteriorate. The onset of
strong gusty winds or flooding can cause certain preparedness
activities to become unsafe.

Be sure to let friends and family members know of your intentions for
weathering the storm and your whereabouts. Have someone located away
from the threatened area serve as your point of contact. Share vital
contact information with others. Keep cell phones handy and charged.

Check on those who may not be fully aware of the situation or who are
unable to make personal preparations.

If you are a visitor, know the name of the county in which you are
located and where it is relative to current watches and warnings. If
staying at a hotel, ask the management staff about their onsite
disaster plan. Listen for evacuation orders, especially pertaining to
area visitors.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather Radio and local news
outlets for official storm information. Listen for possible changes
to the forecast.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Tallahassee FL around 5 PM EDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

properties.description:
* WHAT...Flash flooding caused by excessive rainfall continues to be
possible.

* WHERE...Portions of southeast Alabama, including the following
areas, Geneva and Houston, Florida, including the following areas,
Calhoun, Central Walton, Coastal Bay, Coastal Franklin, Coastal
Gulf, Coastal Jefferson, Coastal Wakulla, Gadsden, Holmes, Inland
Bay, Inland Franklin, Inland Gulf, Inland Jefferson, Inland
Wakulla, Jackson, Leon, Madison, North Walton, Northern Liberty,
South Walton, Southern Liberty and Washington, and Georgia,
including the following areas, Baker, Ben Hill, Berrien, Brooks,
Calhoun, Colquitt, Cook, Decatur, Dougherty, Early, Grady, Irwin,
Lanier, Lee, Lowndes, Miller, Mitchell, Randolph, Seminole,
Terrell, Thomas, Tift, Turner and Worth.

* WHEN...Through Monday evening.

* IMPACTS...Excessive runoff may result in flooding of rivers,
creeks, streams, and other low-lying and flood-prone locations.
Flooding may occur in poor drainage and urban areas.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- Additional rainfall totals of 2 to 4 inches are forecast for most
of the area with locally higher amounts of up to 6 inches
possible through Monday, especially along the Emerald and
Forgotten Coasts. Another area of concern is across south-central
Georgia where locally heavy rainfall since Friday afternoon has
primed the region more so than the rest of our area, so it wont
take as much rain to cause flash flooding. Across the flood watch
area, very high rain rates due to the tropical air mass may lead
to flash flooding, especially in urban and poor drainage areas.
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
properties.instruction:
You should monitor later forecasts and be prepared to take action
should Flash Flood Warnings be issued.

Southwestern Walton County in the panhandle of Florida...
